messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Delgado is a 22-year-old Colombian-American man who works as a junior product manager at a mid-sized tech firm in Austin, Texas. He came to the clinic after months of escalating distress that had begun to affect his performance at work and his relationships with colleagues. His presentation centres on a period he spent as a civilian in a conflict zone in his early twenties — an experience that has left its mark on how his body and mind interpret the world around him.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Mateo was visiting extended family in a rural region of Colombia when the area came under sustained armed conflict. For several days, he and his relatives sheltered in a concrete outbuilding while gunfire and explosions sounded at unpredictable intervals, sometimes close enough to shake the walls. He described lying flat on the ground for hours, certain that any movement or sound might draw attention to their location. At one point, a door burst open without warning — a cousin, not a combatant — and Mateo's body launched itself across the room before he had any conscious thought. That involuntary lurch, he said, was the moment he understood that something inside him had changed.

In the weeks after returning to the United States, Mateo found that his body had not registered the safety of Austin in the way he expected. He described a persistent physical tension that never fully released — muscles braced, jaw clenched, a low-level readiness that he could not switch off. In open-plan office environments, where colleagues moved quickly between desks and chairs scraped unexpectedly across floors, he would startle violently, knocking over his coffee or spinning around from his monitor. He began scanning the room compulsively during meetings, tracking movement near the glass walls of the conference room, unable to follow the product roadmap discussions he was supposed to be leading. He had come to believe that if he stopped watching, something would happen before he could react — a conviction that felt as certain and physical as gravity.

It was this relentless state of alert that first pushed Mateo toward behaviours that he now recognises as harmful. When the tension became unbearable — usually late in the evening after a day of hypervigilance at the office — he began hurting himself physically, pressing his nails hard into his forearm or snapping a rubber band against his wrist with force. He described these moments with a mixture of shame and relief: the sharp, localised pain seemed to interrupt the diffuse, uncontrollable alarm in his body and briefly return him to something he could locate and name. He also began texting friends and his older sister at odd hours, asking whether he seemed okay, whether they thought he was handling things normally, whether he was worrying too much — a pattern of reassurance-seeking that had strained several friendships. And he had developed a habit of checking his body throughout the day, pressing his fingertips to his chest to feel his heartbeat, scanning his arms for signs of injury, running his hands along his sides during bathroom breaks as if confirming he was intact.

The difficulty was that none of these strategies brought lasting relief. The self-harm, the reassurance, the body checking — each provided a momentary reduction in distress, but in the hours that followed, Mateo found himself more attuned to threat than before, as though the act of seeking relief had confirmed to some part of him that there was something real to be relieved from. His body would tighten again, his vigilance would sharpen, and the cycle would close around him. Colleagues had begun to notice that he seemed distracted and on edge, and his manager had gently raised concerns about his focus during a recent one-on-one — a conversation that Mateo found humiliating and that intensified his monitoring of his own reactions throughout the workday.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in a team meeting when an unexpected knock on the glass partition caused him to stand up from his chair involuntarily, drawing stares from the entire room. He sat back down and said nothing, but that evening he called a crisis line and asked for a referral. What he most fears, he said quietly in the intake session, is that his body will never stop waiting for something terrible to happen. What he most hopes is that someone can help him feel safe in his own skin again.
